summary: This work experimentally demonstrates how symmetry-protected topological order in a one-dimensional cluster state prepared on a five-qubit superconducting array manifests differently depending on how measurement and decoherence are applied. By controlling dephasing, measuring sublattices in tunable bases, and selectively discarding measurement records, the authors reveal average symmetry-protected topological order, measurement-induced long-range entanglement, and strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking encoded in the same underlying state.
motivation: Understanding how quantum information and topological order transform under measurement and decoherence is fundamental for open quantum systems and measurement-based quantum computation, yet the controlled interplay between measurement, symmetry, and mixed-state topology has remained largely unexplored experimentally.
method: Five fixed-frequency transmons with tunable nearest-neighbor couplers prepared a five-qubit cluster state via adiabatic CZ gates (fidelities 0.92–0.98). String-order correlations were measured under controlled odd-sublattice dephasing, and measurement-conditioned dynamics were probed by rotating measurement bases on qubits Q2 and Q4 before state tomography on Q1, Q3, Q5.
result: Odd-sublattice dephasing selectively suppressed odd-sublattice strings while preserving even-sublattice string order, consistent with average symmetry-protected topological phases. Measurements in the X basis prepared a GHZ state with 0.667±0.003 fidelity; rotating to π/2 gave a paramagnetic state with 0.888±0.002 fidelity. Discarding measurement records yielded a mixed state with vanishing conventional correlators (e.g., ⟨Z1Z5⟩=0.053) but near-unity fidelity correlators (F15SWSSB=0.949), witnessing strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking.
